title: Joshua 15:1–12
context: Judah receives the first and largest allotment west of the Jordan, and the chapter opens by tracing its four borders: the southern edge toward Edom and the wilderness of Zin, the Salt Sea on the east, a northern line running past Jerusalem to the coast, and the Mediterranean on the west. The careful boundary list shows that God's promise of land to Abraham's offspring is being made concrete, tribe by tribe and place by place.

verses.text: The lot for the tribe of the children of Judah according to their families was to the border of Edom, even to the wilderness of Zin southward, at the uttermost part of the south.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the land comes by lot, yet it arrives as the fulfillment of a promise Israel had to trust and act on. Judah's border reaching toward Edom and Zin shows a gift received in history, not an abstraction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the lot as God's own assignment, since "its every decision is from the LORD" (Proverbs 16:33). Judah's portion, placed first and largest, fits the leadership later promised to Judah in Genesis 49:10.

verses.text: Their south border was from the uttermost part of the Salt Sea, from the bay that looks southward;
verses.arminianNotes: The southern line begins at the tip of the Salt Sea, the Dead Sea. Arminian readers take the precision as a sign that God's promises land in real geography, inviting Israel to settle and steward a specific place in faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note how closely this matches Numbers 34:3, where Moses had already marked the south border "from the end of the Salt Sea." God's word given earlier is carried out exactly as spoken.

verses.text: and it went out southward of the ascent of Akrabbim, and passed along to Zin, and went up by the south of Kadesh Barnea, and passed along by Hezron, went up to Addar, and turned toward Karka;
verses.arminianNotes: Kadesh Barnea on this border recalls where the earlier generation refused to enter (Numbers 14). Arminian readers see a sober reminder that the same gift once rejected in unbelief is now received by a new generation that trusts.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also hear the echo of Kadesh Barnea and stress God's patience: the promise was not canceled by one generation's unbelief but carried forward to their children, as God had said it would be.

verses.text: and it passed along to Azmon, went out at the brook of Egypt; and the border ended at the sea. This shall be your south border.
verses.arminianNotes: The border runs to "the brook of Egypt," a wadi marking the far southwest. Arminian readers note the phrase "This shall be your south border," spoken as an address to Israel, calling them to take up what God assigns.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers connect "the brook of Egypt" with the wide promise of Genesis 15:18, "from the river of Egypt." The allotment is one stage in God keeping the oath he swore to Abraham by covenant.

verses.text: The east border was the Salt Sea, even to the end of the Jordan. The border of the north quarter was from the bay of the sea at the end of the Jordan.
verses.arminianNotes: The east border is the Salt Sea up to the mouth of the Jordan, where the north line begins. Arminian readers see God's ordering of the land as a gracious structure within which each tribe is called to live faithfully.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the borders are set before Judah has secured every town inside them. God defines the inheritance by his word first, and Israel's possession follows within that settled purpose.

verses.text: The border went up to Beth Hoglah, and passed along by the north of Beth Arabah; and the border went up to the stone of Bohan the son of Reuben.
verses.arminianNotes: Beth Hoglah, Beth Arabah, and the stone of Bohan are local landmarks whose exact locations need not be fixed here. Arminian readers note that ordinary features of the land become witnesses to God's faithfulness to his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in these modest landmarks the detailed care of providence. The God who governs nations also marks out stones and villages, and nothing in his people's inheritance is beneath his attention.

verses.text: The border went up to Debir from the valley of Achor, and so northward, looking toward Gilgal, that faces the ascent of Adummim, which is on the south side of the river. The border passed along to the waters of En Shemesh, and ended at En Rogel.
verses.arminianNotes: The line passes the valley of Achor, where Achan was judged (Joshua 7:26). Arminian readers see a warning on Judah's own border: covenant unfaithfulness had real consequences, yet the people moved on in renewed obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers recall that Hosea 2:15 later promises "the valley of Achor for a door of hope." A place tied to judgment on Judah's border becomes, in the prophets, a sign of God's restoring grace.

verses.text: The border went up by the valley of the son of Hinnom to the side of the Jebusite (also called Jerusalem) southward; and the border went up to the top of the mountain that lies before the valley of Hinnom westward, which is at the farthest part of the valley of Rephaim northward.
verses.arminianNotes: The border skirts "the Jebusite (also called Jerusalem)" along the valley of Hinnom. Arminian readers note that Jerusalem, central to Israel's later story, lies here at the edge, still unconquered (verse 63).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the city God would later choose for his name sits on this boundary, still held by others. Hinnom, later a site of idolatrous child sacrifice (2 Kings 23:10), also appears in the line, a hint of struggles to come.

verses.text: The border extended from the top of the mountain to the spring of the waters of Nephtoah, and went out to the cities of Mount Ephron; and the border extended to Baalah (also called Kiriath Jearim);
verses.arminianNotes: The border reaches Baalah, "also called Kiriath Jearim," where the ark would later rest (1 Samuel 7:1). Arminian readers note how the tribal map becomes the stage on which Israel's future faithfulness and failure play out.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 1 Chronicles 13:6 calls Baalah "Kiriath Jearim, which belonged to Judah." The towns named here become places where God's presence among his people is later displayed.

verses.text: and the border turned about from Baalah westward to Mount Seir, and passed along to the side of Mount Jearim (also called Chesalon) on the north, and went down to Beth Shemesh, and passed along by Timnah;
verses.arminianNotes: Beth Shemesh and Timnah lie along this stretch, and Beth Shemesh later receives the returning ark (1 Samuel 6:13). Arminian readers see land and history bound together, the stage for Israel's later faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers trace how God's unfolding plan moves through these named places. The border list is not filler; it sets the stage on which later acts of judgment and deliverance happen under God's hand.

verses.text: and the border went out to the side of Ekron northward; and the border extended to Shikkeron, and passed along to Mount Baalah, and went out at Jabneel; and the goings out of the border were at the sea.
verses.arminianNotes: The line runs near Ekron and out to the sea. Ekron was a Philistine city (Joshua 13:3). Arminian readers note that the border includes land not yet held, calling Judah to future trust and action rather than settled ease.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God assigns Judah territory before it is secured, as with the Philistine plain. The assignment rests on God's promise, and the gradual possession of it unfolds within his timing (compare Deuteronomy 7:22).

verses.text: The west border was to the shore of the great sea. This is the border of the children of Judah according to their families.
verses.arminianNotes: The west border is the Mediterranean, "the great sea." Arminian readers see the closing summary as an invitation: the whole territory is now Judah's to inhabit, cultivate, and guard in covenant faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear in the summary formula "This is the border of the children of Judah" a statement of God's settled allotment. What God has portioned out is secure because it rests on his promise and decision.
